utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, the case number IT-95-8-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sikirica, Dosen, Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you if it please the Court, Dirk Ryneveld along with my co-counsel Daryl Mundis and Julia Baly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Vladimir Petrovic appearing for Damir Dosen, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dusan Vucicevic on behalf of Dragan Kolundzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am Veselih Londrovic appearing on behalf of Mr. Dusko Sikirica. I should also like you to grant the presence of my colleague, Mr. Greaves, who is to be co-counsel in this case. For some technical reasons, the procedure has not been finished for his appointment of the co-counsel, and our interpreter, Mrs. Mirka Kovic [phoen], because I am one of the Defence counsels who do not speak any of the languages of the Court so I should like to ask your leave for our interpreter to be present here to help me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can't see you, Mr. Londrovic. It's not a very well-designed court. Is it going to be very inconvenient for you either to go -- you can either go to the back or you can come in the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. We shall move over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. We can see you and your application is granted, Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I was saying – if you are now on the air – that your application is granted, and we'll begin with your motion on the form of the indictment. We'll deal with that first, and then we'll deal with the motion in relation to adjudicated facts. Again, we'll hear you on that and also the motion on documentary evidence. So we'll deal with things in that order. We've seen your pleading and we've seen the response so we don't need you to repeat any of that. If there's anything you'd like to say in response to the Prosecution, we'll hear you now. I should say that we've got until 5 o’clock for this hearing, and before we close, we must have a Status Conference too. So if people would be brief, we'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I continue to stand by the motion which Mr. Sikirica's counsel submitted on the 14th of August, 2000. I have received the Prosecution's response to our motion concerning the defects in the form of the indictment, and I have nothing new to add. I stand by our motion and I believe that the Chamber will rule on all those motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So I take it you don't want to add anything on the other two motions, of course you can do so. Do you want to say anything about the documentary evidence or the adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the adjudicated facts, I have also submitted to the Court our motion in writing. It was submitted on the 3rd of September this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've seen that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have not yet received the response of the Prosecution to this motion and I, again, stand by this motion of the 3rd of September this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: May I see the Prosecution response? Mr. Ryneveld, have you got a copy of it? No doubt you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure we will be able to find one. I'm sure that it was filed and, therefore, I assume that my learned friend would have received a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just see. It may be that I -- I'm in error there. The original motion was, of course, yours and so the response was Mr. Sikirica's and it may be that we've got no other filings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The only filing I have in the matter was filed on the 7th of August, 2000, which was the Prosecution's motion. Similarly for the documentary evidence, that was also filed on the 7th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And we've got the response from Mr. Sikirica of the 1st of September. Those are the filings. Well, we'll deal firstly -- it may be better to deal with it in order. We'll go back to the motion in relation to the indictment and we'll consider that for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has had the opportunity of considering this matter as it has been pleaded, and our decision is as follows: In relation to the allegations of crimes that occurred outside the Keraterm camp, this was a matter which we've already dealt with in relation to the co-accused, and in the same way as we rejected those motions, we reject this one. It's alleged that the allegations, the indictment, is vague and fails to meet the standards of sufficiency in relation to time and location of the offences of the victims and coperpetrators. Article 18 of the Statute and Rule 47(C) of the Rules require no more than a concise statement of the facts and of the crimes charged, although it must be said that this Trial Chamber has recognised there is a floor below which the level of information must not fall if the indictment is to be valid as to form. Dealing with the decision on preliminary motions issued on the 10th of February in relation of the co-accused, the Trial Chamber required the Prosecution to amend the Attachment A containing more specific information in relation to the crimes charged, and order that it form part of the indictment against those co-accused. For the same reasons, the Trial Chamber now directs the Prosecution to amend Attachment A to specify the time and place of the alleged offences, the identity of the victims and coperpetrators in respect of the charges against Mr. Sikirica which shall form part of the amended indictment against the accused. The Defence now submit that the Prosecution should amend the indictment to provide a factual description of the accused's mens rea in respect of the genocide count and his participation. It's to be noted that Mr. Sikirica is the only accused in this indictment who is accused of genocide and complicity to commit genocide. The indictment simply alleges that he acted with the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in part as, national, ethnic, or religious groups. The indictment refers to a plan to expel those populations from the Prijedor municipality, and it's alleged that it was ordered and implemented by the Bosnian Serb authorities in the Prijedor municipality. The Defence request that the Prosecution provide additional details as to the relationship between the accused and the plan which I have referred to. The Trial Chamber directs the Prosecution to provide these additional details linking Mr. Sikirica as alleged to the plan of the Bosnian Serb authorities. It's next submitted that the Prosecution should provide greater detail as to the identity of those authorities. The Trial Chamber is satisfied that there is sufficient detail for the purposes of the indictment. It's submitted here, it's submitted next, that the Prosecution shall provide more precise information about the accused's participation in the acts underlying the charge against him, and whether his liability is based on Article 7(1) or Article 7(3). The question then is whether the accused is entitled to more detailed information regarding the basis for his liability under these articles. Paragraph 19 of the indictment alleges the accused was the commander of Keraterm camp. As the commander he was in a position of superior authority to everyone else present in the camp. In the Trial Chamber's view, this allegation provides sufficient information as to the basis for the accused's liability under Article 7(3). The Defence next argues that Mr. Sikirica was, in fact, not the commander of the camp. An objection to the form of the indictment is not an appropriate place or proceeding for contesting the accuracy of the facts pleaded, as was set out in our decision in this case of the 10th of February. It is a matter which will have to be dealt with in trial. In relation to Article 7(1), as the Trial Chamber held in its decision of the 10th of February in this case, the form of the alleged participation of the accused is a material averment which should clearly be laid out in the indictment in order to clarify it and make plain the Prosecution case. That being so, the Trial Chamber orders the Prosecution to specify in Attachment A in respect of each incident where the victim, or victims, place and date is identified; the capacity in which each accused is alleged to have participated pursuant to Article 7(1); and where possible, specifying the form of participation, such as planning or instigating or ordering. That is the decision of the Trial Chamber on that motion. The next two motions are Prosecution motions for, first of all, a notice for judicial notice of adjudicated facts against Mr. Sikirica, and also a similar motion for the admission of documentary evidence. There were similar motions, it's to be noted in the case, of the other co-accused. We have the pleadings which I have already been through. Does anybody want to add anything as to what's already pleaded? As I say, we've read them. We've had a chance to consider them. Mr. Ryneveld, these are your motions. Is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Nothing further at this time, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will consider those matters and we'll give a ruling in due course. This brings us to the motion on behalf of Mr. Kolundzija for the production of the statements, the reports, summaries, articles, and books which a witness in this case, Hanne Greve uses in her evidence, her expert evidence. In this connection we have the original motion from Mr. Vucicevic dated the 3rd of August. We have the Prosecution's response of the 18th of August. Mr. Vucicevic, is there anything you want to add, bearing in mind that we've read what's already been said already? Is there anything you want to add to your written pleadings?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour. Just briefly, in the response, the Prosecution indicates that we have not established relevance, and I believe the relevance is indeed obvious because if the expert witness who has been characterised that is akin to a historian but indeed not a historian but testifying for the facts that are at issue here is using the statements of the eyewitnesses. Basically she is just collating those witness statements through her testimony, recycling them if you will. I think you know that what is at issue is going to be her interpretation of those statements and biases are also -- bias is a subject matter to all the investigation of any witness. Therefore, if you can get material, it would be the same thing if she were to testify from a treaties, and we would certainly go to library and get the treaties. I do not understand why any of those reasons would be at issue. That confidentiality of the witnesses or what the witnesses have said. As a matter of fact, you know, I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: -- a lot of witnesses that are victims, that their memory is waning, that some events are being, you know, interposed and what would be a better help to this Trial Chamber in making decisions if he were to review the witness statements that were so close to the events. And yet those -- all those statements are five years old now and even more. So we would undertake that arduous work but we would help, perhaps, if they are -- if there is nothing, you know, to cross-examine based on those statements, we wouldn't raise any points. But I think it would help the cause of justice here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution have pointed to the decision of the Trial Chamber in Kovacevic, in a similar motion, involving the same witness. Now, if we were minded to apply that decision, what would you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm glad the Court noted that objection; however, we have to know the timing because our request in Kovacevic's case, indeed it was my request, at that time, and it was on the eve of the trial. And there was no possible time to gather those information and that was, you know, a week or two just before the trial. Now, we have the trial is set, perhaps might be reset. We have time to get those and we -- I couldn't phrase my request at that time properly because I really didn't know because we had got those -- even statement of the witness just a couple of days before I made that statement. I think you know, we know her testimony. We know that she -- in Kovacevic trial indicated failure to her testimony subject to the -- witnesses --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You are being asked to slow down by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: -- I believe the transcripts in the decision, in the comments of the Court in Kovacevic's case are very pertinent on this issue. And since decision has been rendered before, those comments the Court made, I believe they are indeed very helpful answering and supporting my answer to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ryneveld, is there anything you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just one factor, if I might, and that was with respect to my friend's seemingly expanded request here for notes and transcripts of conferences of other members of the Commission. It was the relevance and probative value of that material that I particularly wanted to bring the Court's attention to with respect to the fact that there could possibly not have any relevance or probative value on the evidence that my -- that she is likely to give. Those are my only comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber will consider these matters and give a ruling in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll turn next to the Status Conference and consider,first of all, the question of readiness for trial. The position is that the trial date has been set, the 6th of November. We will not be minded to move that, it's been set for sometime now. It's important that this trial gets on. We would wish, first of all, to hear about the position in relation to Mr. Sikirica who came much more recently to the Tribunal and would say that, of course, if at all possible, his trial, since he's accused jointly with the other two, his trial should take place at the same time. But perhaps we can start with the Prosecution. Mr. Ryneveld, are you ready for trial in all these matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The issue of readiness for trial, Your Honour, is such that we, of course, have been aware of the date of November 6th for some time, and we would have to take the position that we would be prepared to proceed with our case on the 6th of November. I must, however, point out that if Mr. Sikirica were to join in at that time, and that is another issue, there would have to be some issues with respect to abridgment of time frames, especially in light of the Chamber's ruling today about an amended indictment and matters of that nature. Now, I think we still have some seven weeks prior to that trial date but, for example, our witness list with respect to Mr. Sikirica, our pre-trial brief and our Rule 65 ter with respect to those matters have not yet been filed. You can appreciate too that it would require an abridgment of some of the time limits in order for us to comply with those matters in order to have a trial against all three accused commencing on the 6th of November. A short answer would have to be, the Prosecution is prepared to proceed on the date suggested, but I do understand that there is a concomitant interest, and to save judicial economy, all of those factors have to be taken into account, that it would be preferable if we could start the matter against all three accused. I mean, the witnesses would be pretty much the same, although there would be an expanded witness list if Mr. Sikirica were to, were to be joined in at trial. Nevertheless, there is a balancing act that the Court would have to perform in order to weigh the necessity to proceed on the 6th of November, or to have a separate trial if he were not prepared to proceed. I perhaps have overextended my response, but in a nutshell, if we're proceeding on the 6th of November, the Prosecution will be prepared to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rynveld, the question that was raised by Judge May implies that the trial must open, must start, on the 6th of November for all three accused. There will be no trial for only two accused and then, later on, the third one. So the answer that we are expecting from you is whether you are able to proceed with all of them. You have just quoted Rule 65 ter, and its provisions have to be complied with before the 6th of November, including the amendment which was decided upon today, the amendment of the indictment. That's what we are -- that's what we expect from you, to be ready on the 6th of November. Are you ready to proceed on the 6th of November in respect of all three of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNVELD
utterances.text: With the exception as I've indicated for the necessity for abridgement of time for responses, I believe that we can provide a 65 ter new witness list for witnesses against Sikirica, and a new pre-trial brief. The only difficulties, as I have indicated, is that there may have to be some abridgements of time sought in order to allow us to be ready for trial. But if the question is, can we prepare a list, file a pre-trial brief, do an opening, and have witnesses ready to go on the 6th of November against all three? If we're granted the time within that period, it is, it is our every intention, God willing, that we're able to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you will be ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic -- Mr. Greaves. Well, you know the position: If you're ready on the 6th of November, then the trial can commence; but otherwise, well, we would have to consider the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I open by saying this, that my learned friend didn't, if I may say so, sound to be brimming with confidence, exactly, that he could be ready as against Mr. Sikirica by the 6th of November. Your Honour, our position is this: Mr. Sikirica's case is not ready for trial, and it is not considered that there is any realistic prospect that we could be ready by the date of 6th of November. Your Honour, I'm sure, doesn't need me to lecture the Trial Chamber about the difficulties that are posed by tracing of witnesses in particular, which is one of the big bugbears that any Defence team faces in a case of this kind. In this case, we need to trace witnesses who are located particularly in the Prijedor area, but, in fact, throughout the Republika Srpska entity. We are looking for witnesses in what is known as the federation; in other words, the main part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That proposes particularly problems for any lawyer from Republika Srpska because of obvious difficulties, which I needn't go into, that are faced by someone of that kind. We've also got a situation where we are seeking witnesses outside the area of the former Yugoslavia. That, again, takes some time because lawyers have to get visas and so on and so forth. That's just a general reminder which I hope Your Honours don't mind me making of the problems that are faced in a case of this kind. As far as the material which we've been served with, can I just go through quickly our situation. We received the supporting material. That contained a number of transcripts from former trials and four witness statements. In relation to those matters, we have traced some, but not all, of the witnesses that we would wish to consider as potential Defence witnesses. We have received a first batch of 50 witness statements. That was sometime ago. Again, we have traced some, but not all, potential Defence witnesses arising from those witness statements. My learned friend Mr. Londrovic arrived from Republika Srpska last night and has found in his box a further 38 witness statements in addition to the initial 50. Some of those have yet to be translated into B/C/S, the language with which the accused is familiar and with which my learned friend Mr. Londrovic is familiar. He doesn't speak either English or French. Again, in relation to those new witness statements, of course, because he's only just received them, no investigation has taken place in connection with them. And this afternoon a further three have been served.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, I should like to ask you if you are aware of the provisions of Rule 65 ter (G) which provides as follows; I will read it in English: [English] "... and before the commencement of the defence case, the pre-trial Judge shall order the defence to file the following: (i) a list of witnesses the defence intends to call with:" Et cetera. That means that you are not obliged to give your own list of witnesses before the starting of the trial. You have to be in a position to give your own list after the close of the Prosecutor case, which we have not discussed this yet, but the Prosecutor’s case will take some time. So are you aware of that? Does it change your mind about the possibility of starting on the 6th November, even if your own list is not complete at this date?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sadly not, and for this reason, Your Honour, if I can explain. The Prosecution calls its witnesses, and it may well be that the Defence in the ordinary course of events has its own witnesses who contradict that which the Prosecution witnesses say. And it is for that purpose that the Defence seeks out witnesses of its own, so that it may put to a particular Prosecution witness either that there is some mistake on the witness's part or that the witness is not telling the truth. Until we have interviewed an individual witness about an individual incident related by the Prosecution witness, the Defence is not in a position properly to put its case to that witness, and it is for that reason that we respectfully submit that the Defence is entitled to conclude its investigation before being forced into the situation of having to cross-examine witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we hear about the difficulties; now let's hear about when you will be ready, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, just allow me a moment to complete what I had intended to say. I'll be as brief as I can. I take Your Honour's nod as a "yes." Thank you very much. Your Honour, there is likely to be, in relation to some dates, an alibi notice filed in this case. Again, we found some, but not all, witnesses, and we are not in a position to file a proper full alibi notice at this time. No decision has been taken as to the issue of seeking discovery from the Prosecution under Rule 66(B), and we will not take such a decision until all witness statements, as far as possible, that the Prosecution intend to rely upon are served. It's not a decision that we feel we should take until we have a complete overview of the Prosecution case. We have no idea at the present time what is involved and precisely how much material the Prosecution has in its possession that would be required to be looked at. Your Honour has raised -- or sorry, my learned friend has raised the issue of the amended indictment. That, of course, may pose yet -- may produce yet further requirement to make inquiries, and at the present time, we don't know when the amendments will be forthcoming. It may be that Your Honour is going to order a time by which such amendments must be made. Plainly, the Prosecution is still engaged in the process of investigation. As I was saying when the learned Judge, I'm not going to say "interrupt," "intervened" I think it probably the politer word. We've received three statements today taken in the middle of August. Again, it's plain that investigations are still continuing, and we anticipate there will be yet further statements forthcoming as against Mr. Sikirica. I can now come to the question that Your Honour was posing a moment or two ago. Your Honour will know that I've only just come into the case in the very recent past, but I've discussed the matter of when my learned friend considers that his investigations would be complete and we can file all the appropriate documentation. We were looking at a date rather more in the light of March of next year. Your Honour, we say that -- we are, of course, fully conscious of the difficulties that are faced by witnesses who have to come and give evidence twice and all the logistical difficulties that that might create if there was a to be a separation of Sikirica from the other two, for example. We're also conscious of the fact that if we remain with the other two defendants, then that would cause a delay in their trial. But the fact of the matter is, the defendant was arrested barely four months ago. He has had considerably less time than either the Prosecution or the two co-defendants to prepare their case. That puts him at a significant potential disadvantage vis-à-vis this trial, which is a serious matter in which he is charged with the most serious offence which is contained within the Statute, namely, genocide. Your Honour, that is our position. It is with regret, of course, that we say that we are not in a position to be ready, but in our respectful submission, there are proper reasons why we are not ready. The case is not ready to present to the Court at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, how may I help you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You mentioned March as the earliest date. I was wondering whether it wouldn't be feasible for you to be ready in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The date I have proposed is the one that my learned friend who leads me is the one that he has proposed. He is better acquainted with his preparations in the case, and I take it from him that that is his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps you could give some reconsideration to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Might I just briefly in sotto voce speak with my learned friend through our interpreter and see what his attitude to that is. Would Your Honours permit me to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to cede to my learned friend Mr. Londrovic who, as I have indicated, is much more aware of the state of his preparations than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when we said that the Defence of the accused Sikirica could be ready for the month of March, this was, believe me, really the time framework which was the best that we could offer, and, of course, to the detriment of Mr. Sikirica. Let me give you the reasons for that decision. Bearing in mind all other cases that are pending before the trial, the experience has shown that all Defence teams had between 10 and 12 months to prepare their case from the moment of the arrest of the accused until the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Londrovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. That may be the case, may have been the case in the past, but it is a matter which has really got to be remedied in this Tribunal. We must start getting these cases on. And although there have been delays, that year is not to be taken as a norm of some sort, and in that, Defence counsel have to play their part. But I interrupted you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, anything earlier than March, in our respectful submission, would lead to the violation of Article 21 of the Statute, subparagraph 4(B), where a minimum of rights is guaranteed to the accused, one such right being to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of the defence. We believe that the month of March is the best possible framework that we can suggest and that would be acceptable for us. We are, of course, perfectly aware of the situation in which the other two accused find themselves. I think that Mr. Kolundzija will have been over one year in detention if the trial should begin in November; but if the trial should start in November, we would have had only four months for our preparation. If we decide to start in March, then it means that we will have eight months to prepare for our defence which is an adequate amount of time, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Well, the Trial Chamber will have to consider the position. Quite clearly, if the three accused can be tried together, that would be, in many ways, more satisfactory; but we do have in mind very much the length of time which the other two co-accused have been in custody. So since we are going to have to consider this question of time, we'll hear from anybody else who would like to make submissions. It may be convenient if we hear from the Defence first, and then we'll hear from the Prosecution. Mr. Petrovic, would you like to begin? You've heard what counsel for the co-accused has said, that they won't be ready, it's said, until March. No doubt that might be brought forward to some extent, but it does mean the new year. Now, were we to consider postponing the trial, that would be the trial of your client too. What would your submissions be?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me the floor. There are several things that I should like to mention in respect to this problem. First of all as regards our position, we are ready, as far as the accused Dosen is concerned, to proceed with trial on the 6th of November. Second, I think that it is very important to state that it is in the interests of my client that this trial be held for all three of the accused; that is, that they all be tried together. Third, if a postponing of the trial is going to be discussed, bearing in mind all the reasons and arguments relating to the judicial economy, and also bearing in mind the submissions made by my learned colleagues representing Mr. Sikirica, so if the Chamber should consider the postponing of the date of the 6th of November, we believe that that postponement should be within a reasonable amount of time which would not lead to the accused sitting in detention almost two years or one year respectively. So if there should be a postponement, I should like to appeal to the Chamber to consider a reasonable postponement of time, one to perhaps two months, not more than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I have two very diametrically opposed consideration here. First, I do sympathise deeply with my colleague Londrovic because I have been in a case of the same magnitude before; but at the same time, March 1st would be a 21-month that my client, Mr. Kolundzija, is incarcerated, and we would be ready to proceed to trial on November 6th as scheduled now. And I believe that Judge Robinson's suggestion would be a wise middle of the road to approach. Perhaps there would be some way to accommodate all of these opposing considerations. I would appreciate this greatly. One small remark. I would not be opposed to separating the trial only to a degree where the -- what had happened in Keraterm on my client's shift while he was a shift commander, I wouldn't oppose that to proceed as early as possible, as I indicated before. In that fashion, maybe we could accommodate all of these new contravening considerations. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just a few points, if I may. Addressing Mr. Vucicevic's last comments first. With the greatest of respect, although I can understand him saying that from his client's point of view, he wouldn't mind if that evidence went separate; however, if we were -- that evidence, that whatever happened on either of the other two shift commanders' shifts, is part of the case against Mr. Sikirica, so it couldn't be done in the absence of Mr. Sikirica. So that is not, with the greatest of respect, a practical solution. The second point I wanted to make was that although I completely understand my learned friend Mr. Londrovic's position, nevertheless, it is not in my understanding correct to say that in all other cases, they have had this length of time. In the Foca trial, for example, Mr. Vukovic joined the case fairly late, and the Trial Chamber was faced with the identical situation, and there was a short adjournment, but he joined, I believe, after about four months. The other example I believe happened in March of this year when the Omarska case started, and there was a late arrestee who also joined the proceedings even after it commenced. I don't say that to argue for or against his motion, I simply wanted to set the record straight in terms of the amount of time that I understand some Defence counsel have had in order to prepare their case. I accept at the outset that this accused is charged with genocide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you remind us, please, when he was arrested; when he made his initial appearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: He was arrested on -- Mr. Mundis reminds me he was arrested on June 24th of this year, and his initial appearance was I believe in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, it wasn't that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: July, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the other two accused, can you remind us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps my learned friends can be of assistance. I don't have that at my fingertips. It's in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm being handed it by the legal officer helpfully. In the case of Mr. Kolundzija, he made an appearance in June of 1999; and the case of Mr. Dosen, November of last year. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The final comment, I think, is perhaps a reiteration of what I said earlier, and that is that I appreciate that the Court has a very difficult balancing to perform in terms of the interest of proceeding as quickly as possible in this matter, and the also obvious judicial public interest in having this case proceed against all three so that the number of witnesses don't have to come yet another time. Some of these witnesses, because of the -- because of the fact that there is -- some of these witnesses also have testified in Omarska. Some of these witnesses -- in other words, to keep bringing these people back because they have evidence on similar matters is very difficult. One might say, well, perhaps, use of affidavits or statements or written testimony may be a solution. In some cases, even that won't be, because the questions that have been asked of them have been limited to their evidence with respect to that particular case, and there is evidence yet to be called from them in respect to Keraterm. So we've looked at all these possibilities, and I must tell you that I'm not asking for an adjournment. We're prepared, with the restrictions that I said before about we're already outside our 60 days that we have to provide certain things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we were minded to vacate the 6th of November in light of the arguments which have been raised on behalf of Mr. Sikirica, when would you invite us to list the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would have to indicate as soon as possible, that is, in compliance with the ability of other counsel to already be ready. If the Court were to consider January or mid-January, I would hope that my learned friend could -- and we would do everything we can in order to facilitate in getting all the documents as soon as possible. But, of course, that depends on Mr. Londrovic's ability to get ready for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter. Perhaps the legal officer could come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, as counsel have rightly indicated, the recent addition to this indictment, or rather, the recent arrest of Mr. Sikirica and, therefore, his appearance to stand his trial on this indictment, of course, which he was already joined in, presents the difficulty that the trial date of the 6th of November had been set, and the case was ready for trial. If I may say, it is a problem peculiar to this Tribunal, I think, but a pressing one for the Tribunal when accused are arrested at different times and appear on the same indictment. It does mean that Trial Chambers have to consider whether it's possible, whether it's right, to go on with the trial as listed. That is particularly pressing when one or more of the accused has been in custody for a long time. In the case of Mr. Kolundzija, he has been in custody since June of 1999; as I said, Mr. Dosen since November of 1999. That is a long time, and their trials should be brought forward as rapidly as possible. On the other hand, we have to balance against that the desirability of trying people on the same -- accused on the same indictment at the same time. And in particular, again, peculiar to this Tribunal, we have witnesses who come from a long way, who, it may be, have to give very distressing evidence, and to force them through that ordeal more than necessary is one of the matters which have to be taken into account. The date of the 6th of November having been fixed for the trial of two of the accused, the arrival of the third accused means that the matter must be reconsidered. We've heard what counsel says for Mr. Sikirica about the difficulties which they are having in preparing his case. We take account of those difficulties and we balance that against the delays which have occurred in trying the other two accused. We think, first of all, for the reasons I have mentioned, that all three should be tried together. We notice that Mr. Petrovic is of that view, as are the Prosecution. We then have to consider how that is to be dealt with. In the light of the difficulties which Mr. Sikirica's Defence are having, and the fact that they are not ready for trial, the date of the 6th of November will be vacated. We then have to consider what an appropriate date for trial would be. Well, the balancing act I've already -- the balancing act which has to be performed is to decide what is fair between all parties in the case having regard to the time which the other accused have been waiting, the fact that the others will be ready for trial, the fact the Prosecution will be ready for trial, and the difficulties which have been outlined in the case of Mr. Sikirica. Balancing all those matters in mind, we agree with the submissions of Mr. Petrovic and indeed supported by the Prosecution that January would be a reasonable time. We heard mid-January suggested. In fact, what we have in mind is to fix the date for this trial as the 22nd of January. That should enable, in our view, Mr. Sikirica to be ready for trial. He will have had more than six months to be ready for trial, and I hope that given the circumstances of this case and the problems which are faced by the two co-accused and the time that they have been in custody, counsel will ensure that they are ready – which they must be – for the 22nd. So the date will be refixed for that date. The 6th of November is vacated. There are a series of other dates which have to be fitted in but it may be more convenient rather than trying to do that on the bench, if we spend little time considering it and we will fix the dates for the attachment to the indictment, the pre-trial brief, and any other consequent matters in a time table which we will announce or we will let you have in as short a time as possible. Mr. Ryneveld, we ought to give you the opportunity of saying how long do you want for the attachment and the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I think we could probably get the attachment done within two weeks. The new pre-trial brief, I would need a little bit longer than that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have to -- two weeks, we'll say that now for the attachment. Pre-trial brief, give us some idea of what you're asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I wonder if I could have an additional two weeks after that, because we have to work all of these things into the pre-trial brief, give a factual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. An additional two weeks for that. And any additional matters we'll give a ruling, we'll make a scheduling order for.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that Your Honour has indicated that you will be providing a scheduling order for the other matters. There is just one other issue which I don't know whether the Court would be taking into consideration and that is -- excuse me one moment. As intimated in the existing 65 ter witnesses and indeed in our pre-trial brief, we have indicated that we will be filing a different list of witnesses in a combined trial. This is not an additional list, I should hasten to add. There will be -- in other words, just because we have a list of witnesses that we would have called for the two accused, if we were calling different witnesses for Sikirica, we might, in fact, replace some of the different witnesses. It's important that we delete some. So perhaps the Court might also give us an indication of timing for the filing of the new 65 ter witness list as well. We are, as my friends have already indicated, in the middle of the investigation process of those additional witnesses. As you may be aware, the present trial team inherited this case from the previous trial team about the 8th of July, and simply by inheriting a file doesn't mean that the process of osmosis gives us the institutional knowledge of the previous trial team. So we have been finding out the history of the trial and interviewing new witnesses with respect to Mr. Sikirica's arrival, and we would need an adequate amount of time in order to prepare the appropriate 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. How long are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I would ask that you have already granted us the extent of basically two weeks followed by another two weeks with the filing of the pre-trial brief. Perhaps we could file the 65 ter list and the pre-trial brief at about the same time which would give us a month in total because the two will have to be intermeshed. I'm not asking for additional time. I'm just trying to get a date set.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right thank you. Yes, we'll agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: That means, Mr. Ryneveld, that with the list of witnesses, you will also provide the list of exhibits at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Yes? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would seem one way or another to do precisely what I said we wouldn't, provide the dates. Let me see if there are any others which we should be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Might I also just add that we will be filing one pre-trial brief for all three as opposed to one separate one for Sikirica because it's going to be a blended one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we would encourage you to do that. We would encourage you to specify precisely how it is you say that each accused is guilty of the offences. I have known pre-trial briefs which do not address the absolutely fundamental issue of what the case is against each accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That is our challenge, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is, at the moment, a requirement that Messrs. Kolundzija and Dosen produce a pre-trial brief on the 2nd of October. That date clearly will be vacated until you have had a chance of seeing the standard pre-trial brief from the Prosecution. Now, unless there are any other matters relating to trial -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one other matter that should come up for clarification, and that is which indictment are we actually dealing with all along? Because as you may have noticed in some of the pleadings, my friends have, of course, referred to section numbers or paragraph numbers in what we call the "extracted indictments". There was originally an indictment naming seven indictees and then an extracted one for Kolundzija and Dosen, we've got the extracted one with different paragraph numbers. And for ease of reference we are assuming that the indictment that we will be dealing with from now on will, in fact, be the original indictment which is the seven indictees. I think that needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That must clearly be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But in order that there is no difficulty about this, it may be sensible for you to serve that indictment again, redacted as necessary, if any redaction is necessary, for the other four. In fact, it is, thinking aloud for a moment. What we want is an indictment, the original indictment with those parts which relate to these three accused in it. It would be helpful if you would serve such a document so that we are all in a position to proceed from the same indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, as Mr. Mundis has informed me that the Confirming Judge has in fact lifted the confidentiality of that seven indictee indictment. So it is now the -- it was the original document, and the reason for the extractions was because it had been deemed, by virtue of an order, to be confidential. We couldn't use it. That's why we had to create extractions for service upon various people. If I understand Your Honour now, what you are asking for is for us to further redact the seven indictee indictment and to eliminate the other four so that we've got an indictment against three and serve that afresh upon the Defence counsel for all three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to me the simplest or the clearest way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, does anybody want to raise anything about that? I mean, it seems sensible to have an indictment on which only these three appear for the purposes of the trial. It's just an easier document to handle for everybody, but it would be the original indictment with the other four accused redacted from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was about to fully endorse what you have just said, but I should like to draw attention to something we discussed this morning with our learned friends from the Prosecution, and that is that between the indictment which so far was the indictment of my client and the indictment of the seven accused, there is some differences, and they go beyond purely formal differences. They go beyond the fact that on this indictment, there is one person, and on that, seven. I may have mentioned that there are quite a number of divergencies between them, that is, my client is related to -- is associated with quite a number of crimes, for instance. In this indictment of seven indictees, for the first time we see the name of the victim against whom my client has allegedly committed crimes, but this is the first time that we see this. And this is the first time that we have to deal with that. That is, there are differences and divergencies as to the substance rather than form only. So we hope that in the new indictment, all these matters will be clarified, clearly defined, so that we really can know what indictment is the basis of the charges and on the basis of what our clients are being tried. I think this is really of paramount importance for all of us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it seems to me that if the Confirming Judge has removed the confidentiality requirement of the indictment, of the original indictment which is confirmed, that was the jurisdiction of the Confirming Judge. And if such a document is available, then it wouldn't serve a purpose to compare and contrast and have the witnesses identify real perpetrators of what had happened in Keraterm. Your Honours have addressed a piecemeal arrest in this case. The Prosecutor has had five years to arrest all seven, and for whatever reason -- I'm not suggesting a lack of due diligence -- but for whatever reason, that didn't occur. And justice would be served, perhaps, if my client or the witnesses that would testify against him would get the chance to pinpoint perhaps if the Prosecutor is mistaken of charging him for certain acts, to assign those acts to the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you're saying that all seven names should remain on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, because the time has passed for confidentiality, and with due respect, it would be a little overextending jurisdiction of the Trial Judge upon this Chamber of the Confirming Judge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider that. Mr. Greaves, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, at one stage I had an urge to say something, but I am now repented of it, and I'm sure everybody is grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the suggestion is we have all seven names on so anybody can identify any other accused. If that's the wish of counsel, it seems to me unobjectionable, and we'll go on going on with the original indictment, then. I think now that really does conclude all matters which we have to deal with in open session except for this, that I make this announcement now so that it's plain, that Judge Bennouna will be presiding over the trial. Now, that leaves some matters which it may be better that are dealt with in private session. If we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 5 p.m. 25
